OTHER SIMPLE EXCISION METHODS The standard elliptical excision may not be suitable for excision of skin lesions in certain age groups and anatomical sites. In such situation, different excision techniques are utilized to give good cosmetic result with minimal scarring.
Circular Excision and Purse-String Closure It is an effective technique used for excision of circular facial skin lesions in children. Apart from infantile hemangioma (at any stage of evolution), other skin lesions treated successfully with this technique include Spitz nevus, pyogenic granuloma, pilomatricoma, vascular malformations and pigmented nevus. 14 In infantile hemangioma, circular excision and purse-string closure converts large circular lesion into a small ellipsoid scar by significantly reducing the transverse and longitudinal dimensions of the lesion. If required, the ellipsoid scar can be revised subsequently to a linear scar of same length. Hence, the smallest possible scar with minimal distortion of surrounding tissue can be achieved by this method.15 However, to avoid pleat formation, this method is not indicated for lesions on the free margins such as periorbital region, or on the upper or lower lip.16

Intralesional Excision and Primary Closure The long scar and dog ear formation of elliptical excision and pleat formation of circular excision can be overcome by intralesional excision and primary closure. Infantile hemangiomas, involuting or involuted, are suitable for intralesional excision because of expanded dome-shaped tissue, and excess and redundant skin which permit easy scooping of fibrofatty tissue and closure of wound edge without tension, respectively. In this method, intralesional elliptical resection with dull apical angles and primary closure is performed without extending the incision into the normal skin. A small outermost portion of the lesion is preserved intentionally. If the residual lesion is large, then the same procedure can be repeated 2–3 times at the interval of 3 months each. Intralesional excision is not indicated for hemangiomas in proliferative phase because of excessive intraoperative bleeding and brittle residual tissue.16
POSTOPERATIVE CARE AND WOUND DRESSING Postoperatively the wound is cleaned to remove blood and residual antiseptic. Dressing is applied in four layers comprising of occlusive ointment, a nonadherent gauze material, an absorbent cushion made of cotton covered with gauze material on both sides and adhesive tape to secure the dressing (Fig. 20). Dressing must kept dry all the time and the patient is instructed accordingly. If the dressing gets soiled it has to be replaced immediately. First redressing is to be done after 24 hours. The patient is trained to do subsequent dressings on his own till suture removal.
COMPLICATIONS AND THEIR MANAGEMENT3 With good planning technique and aseptic precautions, complications in cutaneous surgery are very rare. Patients should be warned and informed about them preoperatively. The surgeon should be able to recognize and manage them whenever they occur.
Hematoma Hematomas are seen within 24–48 hours after surgery and they manifest as swelling, erythema and tenderness at wound site. Hematomas are evacuated promptly by partially or completely opening the wound. Resuturing can be done if hematoma develops within early 24 hours provided the wound is not infected. Otherwise the wound is kept open and allowed to heal by second intention. Scar revision can be done at later date. Very small hematomas need not be opened; they can be managed with warm compresses till resolution.

Dehiscence The wound pulls apart in dehiscence usually as a result of underlying infection and/or hematoma. These causes should be promptly managed allowing the wound to heal by second intention. Delayed scar revision can be done at a later date.
Linear Repair This is simple, easy to perform and useful when it is desirable to extend the excision in a straight line. The apex of tissue protrusion is elevated with a skin-hook to define the geometry of tissue protrusion in the shape of a standing cone. The apex of the cone is drawn to one side so that the base of the tissue protrusion is in line with the long axis of the anticipated wound closure. The base is incised and undermined to free up a triangular wedge of tissue. The triangular section is then draped over the underlying wound edge with gentle tension and the base is incised over the line of closure. The wound is then repaired in a straight line. Other methods of dog-ear repair are curved repair, hockey stick repair, l-shaped repair, T-shaped repair and N-plasty repair.3
Necrosis Necrosis is a rare complication of simple excision surgery. It occurs only if the wound is closed under high tension thereby compromising the vascularity of the wound margins. The course of action should be suture removal, debridement of the necrotic tissue and allowing the wound to heal by second intention. Corrective scar revision is undertaken at a later date.

Dog-ear A skin protrusion present at the end of excision is commonly referred to as a dog-ear. These protrusions are caused by the presence of redundant skin at the ends or dressing sites of an excision. The amount of tissue protrusion formed in a given wound is fundamentally determined by the amount of rotation, advancement and intrinsic tissue elasticity of the surrounding skin. The local surface contours also contribute to the final degree of tissue protrusion. Circumferential closures performed on highly convex surfaces, such as the arm, will result in tissue protrusions at the end of the closure. If excess subcutaneous fat is present at the apex of an excision, the resultant elevation of the angle of closure may mimic a tissue protrusion. Removal of excess

ONJ has developed after as few as 4 months of IV BIS therapy, but the median duration of BIS therapy ranged from 22 to 39 months and the average ranged from 9 to 14 months. The cumulative hazard increased the longer the drug is used.10 Zometa appears to have the greatest risk, as one study reported that 10% of 211 patients receiving the drug developed ONJ compared with 4% of 413 patients who were given Aredia.14 ONJ has developed in both the mandible and the maxilla, although the mandible is the most common oral location. Risk Factors for BRONJ The American Academy of Oral Medicine has published a consensus article with recommendations for the management of clients who have taken BIS.15 They caution practitioners that much is unknown about risk factors for the condition and so little is known about the causative factors that it is unknown how to prevent the condition. Because the current recommendations are not based on randomized studies of the condition, but rather on the experience of a variety of oral surgeons who have managed numerous cases, it is consensus based and may change as more information becomes available.

The most important predisposing factors for the development of BRONJ involve the form of the drug administered and the duration of therapy; and a history of trauma, oral surgery, or oral infection. Periodontal disease has been associated with the development of ONJ in patients who received IV BIS therapy.16 This is a strong factor in favor of maintaining a healthy periodontal and dental condition. Other less common risk factors include former administration of corticosteroid therapy or chemotherapeutic drugs, diabetes, smoking, use of alcohol, and poor oral hygiene. A troubling feature of some reports, however, is of ONJ developing in clients with no dental disease or recent oral surgery, and who took BIS therapy.

Guidance
1. Clinical definitions and laboratory  
diagnosis  
Case  and  outbreak definitions
To  help  in identifying  and  managing  incidents of CDI, the following definitions are  
recommended, which are modified from examples provided in the literature (Department of  
Health, 1994; Jernigan and others  , 1998; Lee, 2006; Healthcare  Commission, 2006a; Musher  
and others, 2006):
•  C. difficile infection: one episode of diarrhoea, defined either as stool loose enough  
to take the shape of a container used to sample it or as Bristol Stool Chart types 5  
to 7 (Appendix 1), that is not attributable to any other cause, including medicines  
(Appendix 2), and that occurs at the same time as a positive toxin assay (with or  
without a positive C. difficile  culture) and/or endoscopic evidence of  
pseudomembranous colitis  
•  a period of increased incidence (PII) of CDI: 2  or more new cases (occurring  more  
than 48 hours post-admission, not relapses) in a 28-  day period  in the same  
location, such as a  hospital ward  
•  an outbreak of CDI  : 2 or more cases caused by the same strain related in time and  
place over a defined period that is based on the date  of onset of the  first  case
The incidence of CDI may differ markedly from one hospital to another. T  rusts  should actively  
manage levels of CDI, whether there is an outbreak against a background of low incidence or  
there is hyperendemic CDI. It is not acceptable for trusts with many CDI cases to set a high  
threshold for response. [2025 expert review: retained with updated text.]

## [PDF page 11]
It is also important to be aware of the ‘background rate’ of diarrhoea in each ward, particularly  
wards with elderly patients, since loose stools are common in this group. An annual rate of 30 to  
35% for episodes among residents in nursing and care homes has been observed  (Department  
of Health, 1994; Musher and others  , 2007). IPCT  s should take a measured approach when  
assessing potential outbreaks of CDI  . Apparent increases in cases may be influenced by factors  
such as improved case ascertainment, heightened clinical awareness, or changes in patient  
population (for example  more high-  risk admissions). These may result in clusters or pseudo-  
outbreaks that do not reflect true transmission events. Outbreak declaration should be based on  
local surveillance data, epidemiological investigation, and in accordance with current guidelines.  
[2025 expert review: retained with updated text.]

To convert the rate per 10,000 patient-days to the rate per 1,000 patient-days, divide the rate by 10 (con-versely, to convert a rate from 1,000 patient-days to 10,000 patient-days, multiply the rate by 10). d. Because of a lack of published data on CDI surveil-lance using similar case-finding methods and surveillance definitions, specific definitions for what constitutes an “outbreak” or “hyperendemic” rate cannot be provided at this time.
i. An outbreak can be defined as an increase in CDI rate in time and/or space believed to be greater than that expected by chance alone.
ii. A hyperendemic rate can be defined as a persis-tently elevated CDI rate compared with past rates or compared with rates in other, similar healthcare facilities.

## section 3: strategies to prevent cdi
1. Existing guidelines and recommendations a. Published guidelines for the management of CDI are few, and only some address CDI prevention. 22,25-27
i. Most data published on CDI prevention are from before-after studies conducted in response to outbreaks. Often, several concomitant interventions are performed, making it difficult to determine the relative importance of one intervention compared with another. Before-after studies are also limited by time-related biases that are difficult to adjust for in the absence of a control group or properly conducted analyses, such as interrupted time series analysis. 30,31 However, 2 recent studies have used these techniques, demonstrating the importance of an-timicrobial stewardship and its role in preventing CDI. 31,32 b. Less is known about the mechanisms and prevention of C. difficile transmission, compared with other antimi-crobial-resistant gram-positive organisms, such as MRSA and vancomycin-resistant enterococcus (VRE). Although these 3 organisms have many common epidemiologic char-acteristics, C. difficile and VRE, in particular, share risk factors for transmission. 33 The major difference among these 3 organisms is that C. difficile forms spores, whereas the other 2 do not. The formation of spores has novel (as yet unknown) implications for methods of hand hygiene and environmental disinfection, because C. difficile spores are resistant to the bactericidal effects of alcohol and most hospital disinfectants. S84 infection control and hospital epidemiology october 2008, vol. 29, supplement 1
c. General strategies to prevent CDI, per previously pub-lished guidelines, 22,24-27 include the following:
i. Methods of reducing the risk of CDI if the organism is encountered by the patient (a) Follow antimicrobial usage restriction and stewardship guidelines.
ii. Methods of preventing the patient from being ex-posed to C. difficile (disinfection and barrier methods) (a) Avoid the use of electronic thermometers; the handles become contaminated with C. difficile.

# 10,000 p rate per 10,000 patient-days. 19
## section 3: strategies to prevent cdi
(b) Use dedicated patient care items and equip-ment; if items must be shared, clean and disinfect the equipment between patients. (c) Use full barrier precautions (gowns and gloves) for contact with patients with CDI and for contact with their body substances and environment (contact precautions). (d) Place patients with CDI in private rooms, if available; give isolation preference to patients with fecal incontinence if room availability is limited. (e) Perform meticulous hand hygiene based on Centers for Disease Control and Prevention or World Health Organization guidelines before and after en-tering the room of a patient with CDI, with soap and water or an alcohol-based hand-hygiene product (in routine settings or settings of endemicity). Perform hand hygiene with soap and water preferentially, in-stead of alcohol hand hygiene products, after caring for a patient with CDI in outbreak settings or settings of hyperendemicity. Ensure that proper hand-hygiene techniques are used when hand washing with soap and water is employed. 34 (f) Perform environmental decontamination of rooms housing patients with CDI, using sodium hypochlorite (household bleach) diluted 1 : 10 with water, in an outbreak setting or setting of hyper-endemicity. (g) Educate healthcare personnel and hospital ad-ministration about the clinical features, transmission, and epidemiology of CDI. d. Other important principles to be aware of when car-ing for patients with CDI include the following: 22,25-27
i. Perform testing for C. difficile only on unformed diarrheal stools (toxin testing of formed stool is strongly discouraged).
ii. Do not give prophylactic antimicrobial CDI ther-apy (eg, with metronidazole or vancomycin) to patients at high risk for CDI.
iii. Do not treat or attempt to decolonize asymptom-atic C. difficile carriers. Antimicrobial therapy is not ef-fective for decolonization.
iv. Do not conduct repeated testing for C. difficile if a patient has had a stool sample positive for C. difficile,
unless symptoms resolved with treatment and then re-turned after treatment (ie, do not perform test of cure in patients successfully treated for CDI). 2. Infrastructure requirements a. Trained infection prevention and control personnel

# 10,000 p rate per 10,000 patient-days. 19
## section 3: strategies to prevent cdi
i. Infection prevention and control personnel must have knowledge about risk factors for and methods to prevent CDI. They must also be trained in how to de-termine when a case of CDI is healthcare associated and how to calculate CDI rates. 20,21 b. Method to identify patients with CDI
i. Infection prevention and control personnel must be able to identify patients with CDI as soon as possible after their condition is diagnosed. This is necessary to ensure that patients are placed under contact precautions in a timely fashion. These data can also be used to cal-culate CDI rates. c. Ability to place patients with CDI under contact precautions
i. Contact precautions require the ability to place pa-tients in a private room (preferably) or to cohort patients with CDI, as well as to place materials necessary for compliance with contact precautions (eg, gowns and gloves) in an easily accessible space outside of the pa-tient’s room.
ii. Place a sign indicating that the patient is under contact precautions outside of the patient’s room.
iii. If there is a limited number of single-bed rooms, patients with stool incontinence should preferentially be placed in these rooms.
iv. If it is necessary to cohort patients, cohort patients who are colonized or infected with the same organism(s) (eg, do not cohort patients with CDI who are discordant in their VRE or MRSA colonization status).
v. Have systems in place to facilitate communication among infection prevention and control, admitting, nursing, and housekeeping departments and develop contingency plans for conditions of limited bed availability. d. Provide educational materials for patients, family members, and healthcare personnel that include explana-tions of CDI, why contact precautions are necessary, and the importance of hand hygiene. e. Provide adequate resources and training for house-keeping personnel to ensure proper cleaning of rooms. 3. Initiating a CDI prevention program a. Pilot test the intervention in 1 patient care location to assess efficacy.
i. Perform CDI surveillance to determine locations where CDI rates are highest.
ii. Initiate the prevention program where there is a high concentration of patients at risk for CDI, such as an intensive care unit or an oncology ward.

Guidance
1. Clinical definitions and laboratory  
diagnosis  
Case  and  outbreak definitions
To  help  in identifying  and  managing  incidents of CDI, the following definitions are  
recommended, which are modified from examples provided in the literature (Department of  
Health, 1994; Jernigan and others  , 1998; Lee, 2006; Healthcare  Commission, 2006a; Musher  
and others, 2006):
•  C. difficile infection: one episode of diarrhoea, defined either as stool loose enough  
to take the shape of a container used to sample it or as Bristol Stool Chart types 5  
to 7 (Appendix 1), that is not attributable to any other cause, including medicines  
(Appendix 2), and that occurs at the same time as a positive toxin assay (with or  
without a positive C. difficile  culture) and/or endoscopic evidence of  
pseudomembranous colitis  
•  a period of increased incidence (PII) of CDI: 2  or more new cases (occurring  more  
than 48 hours post-admission, not relapses) in a 28-  day period  in the same  
location, such as a  hospital ward  
•  an outbreak of CDI  : 2 or more cases caused by the same strain related in time and  
place over a defined period that is based on the date  of onset of the  first  case
The incidence of CDI may differ markedly from one hospital to another. T  rusts  should actively  
manage levels of CDI, whether there is an outbreak against a background of low incidence or  
there is hyperendemic CDI. It is not acceptable for trusts with many CDI cases to set a high  
threshold for response. [2025 expert review: retained with updated text.]

## [PDF page 11]
It is also important to be aware of the ‘background rate’ of diarrhoea in each ward, particularly  
wards with elderly patients, since loose stools are common in this group. An annual rate of 30 to  
35% for episodes among residents in nursing and care homes has been observed  (Department  
of Health, 1994; Musher and others  , 2007). IPCT  s should take a measured approach when  
assessing potential outbreaks of CDI  . Apparent increases in cases may be influenced by factors  
such as improved case ascertainment, heightened clinical awareness, or changes in patient  
population (for example  more high-  risk admissions). These may result in clusters or pseudo-  
outbreaks that do not reflect true transmission events. Outbreak declaration should be based on  
local surveillance data, epidemiological investigation, and in accordance with current guidelines.

## section 3: strategies to prevent cdi
1. Existing guidelines and recommendations a. Published guidelines for the management of CDI are few, and only some address CDI prevention. 22,25-27
i. Most data published on CDI prevention are from before-after studies conducted in response to outbreaks. Often, several concomitant interventions are performed, making it difficult to determine the relative importance of one intervention compared with another. Before-after studies are also limited by time-related biases that are difficult to adjust for in the absence of a control group or properly conducted analyses, such as interrupted time series analysis. 30,31 However, 2 recent studies have used these techniques, demonstrating the importance of an-timicrobial stewardship and its role in preventing CDI. 31,32 b. Less is known about the mechanisms and prevention of C. difficile transmission, compared with other antimi-crobial-resistant gram-positive organisms, such as MRSA and vancomycin-resistant enterococcus (VRE). Although these 3 organisms have many common epidemiologic char-acteristics, C. difficile and VRE, in particular, share risk factors for transmission. 33 The major difference among these 3 organisms is that C. difficile forms spores, whereas the other 2 do not. The formation of spores has novel (as yet unknown) implications for methods of hand hygiene and environmental disinfection, because C. difficile spores are resistant to the bactericidal effects of alcohol and most hospital disinfectants. S84 infection control and hospital epidemiology october 2008, vol. 29, supplement 1
c. General strategies to prevent CDI, per previously pub-lished guidelines, 22,24-27 include the following:
i. Methods of reducing the risk of CDI if the organism is encountered by the patient (a) Follow antimicrobial usage restriction and stewardship guidelines.
ii. Methods of preventing the patient from being ex-posed to C. difficile (disinfection and barrier methods) (a) Avoid the use of electronic thermometers; the handles become contaminated with C. difficile.

(b) Use dedicated patient care items and equip-ment; if items must be shared, clean and disinfect the equipment between patients. (c) Use full barrier precautions (gowns and gloves) for contact with patients with CDI and for contact with their body substances and environment (contact precautions). (d) Place patients with CDI in private rooms, if available; give isolation preference to patients with fecal incontinence if room availability is limited. (e) Perform meticulous hand hygiene based on Centers for Disease Control and Prevention or World Health Organization guidelines before and after en-tering the room of a patient with CDI, with soap and water or an alcohol-based hand-hygiene product (in routine settings or settings of endemicity). Perform hand hygiene with soap and water preferentially, in-stead of alcohol hand hygiene products, after caring for a patient with CDI in outbreak settings or settings of hyperendemicity. Ensure that proper hand-hygiene techniques are used when hand washing with soap and water is employed. 34 (f) Perform environmental decontamination of rooms housing patients with CDI, using sodium hypochlorite (household bleach) diluted 1 : 10 with water, in an outbreak setting or setting of hyper-endemicity. (g) Educate healthcare personnel and hospital ad-ministration about the clinical features, transmission, and epidemiology of CDI. d. Other important principles to be aware of when car-ing for patients with CDI include the following: 22,25-27
i. Perform testing for C. difficile only on unformed diarrheal stools (toxin testing of formed stool is strongly discouraged).
ii. Do not give prophylactic antimicrobial CDI ther-apy (eg, with metronidazole or vancomycin) to patients at high risk for CDI.
iii. Do not treat or attempt to decolonize asymptom-atic C. difficile carriers. Antimicrobial therapy is not ef-fective for decolonization.
iv. Do not conduct repeated testing for C. difficile if a patient has had a stool sample positive for C. difficile,
unless symptoms resolved with treatment and then re-turned after treatment (ie, do not perform test of cure in patients successfully treated for CDI). 2. Infrastructure requirements a. Trained infection prevention and control personnel

## section 3: strategies to prevent cdi
i. Infection prevention and control personnel must have knowledge about risk factors for and methods to prevent CDI. They must also be trained in how to de-termine when a case of CDI is healthcare associated and how to calculate CDI rates. 20,21 b. Method to identify patients with CDI
i. Infection prevention and control personnel must be able to identify patients with CDI as soon as possible after their condition is diagnosed. This is necessary to ensure that patients are placed under contact precautions in a timely fashion. These data can also be used to cal-culate CDI rates. c. Ability to place patients with CDI under contact precautions
i. Contact precautions require the ability to place pa-tients in a private room (preferably) or to cohort patients with CDI, as well as to place materials necessary for compliance with contact precautions (eg, gowns and gloves) in an easily accessible space outside of the pa-tient’s room.
ii. Place a sign indicating that the patient is under contact precautions outside of the patient’s room.
iii. If there is a limited number of single-bed rooms, patients with stool incontinence should preferentially be placed in these rooms.
iv. If it is necessary to cohort patients, cohort patients who are colonized or infected with the same organism(s) (eg, do not cohort patients with CDI who are discordant in their VRE or MRSA colonization status).
v. Have systems in place to facilitate communication among infection prevention and control, admitting, nursing, and housekeeping departments and develop contingency plans for conditions of limited bed availability. d. Provide educational materials for patients, family members, and healthcare personnel that include explana-tions of CDI, why contact precautions are necessary, and the importance of hand hygiene. e. Provide adequate resources and training for house-keeping personnel to ensure proper cleaning of rooms. 3. Initiating a CDI prevention program a. Pilot test the intervention in 1 patient care location to assess efficacy.
i. Perform CDI surveillance to determine locations where CDI rates are highest.
ii. Initiate the prevention program where there is a high concentration of patients at risk for CDI, such as an intensive care unit or an oncology ward.

Guidance
1. Clinical definitions and laboratory  
diagnosis  
Case  and  outbreak definitions
To  help  in identifying  and  managing  incidents of CDI, the following definitions are  
recommended, which are modified from examples provided in the literature (Department of  
Health, 1994; Jernigan and others  , 1998; Lee, 2006; Healthcare  Commission, 2006a; Musher  
and others, 2006):
•  C. difficile infection: one episode of diarrhoea, defined either as stool loose enough  
to take the shape of a container used to sample it or as Bristol Stool Chart types 5  
to 7 (Appendix 1), that is not attributable to any other cause, including medicines  
(Appendix 2), and that occurs at the same time as a positive toxin assay (with or  
without a positive C. difficile  culture) and/or endoscopic evidence of  
pseudomembranous colitis  
•  a period of increased incidence (PII) of CDI: 2  or more new cases (occurring  more  
than 48 hours post-admission, not relapses) in a 28-  day period  in the same  
location, such as a  hospital ward  
•  an outbreak of CDI  : 2 or more cases caused by the same strain related in time and  
place over a defined period that is based on the date  of onset of the  first  case
The incidence of CDI may differ markedly from one hospital to another. T  rusts  should actively  
manage levels of CDI, whether there is an outbreak against a background of low incidence or  
there is hyperendemic CDI. It is not acceptable for trusts with many CDI cases to set a high  
threshold for response. [2025 expert review: retained with updated text.]

## [PDF page 11]
It is also important to be aware of the ‘background rate’ of diarrhoea in each ward, particularly  
wards with elderly patients, since loose stools are common in this group. An annual rate of 30 to  
35% for episodes among residents in nursing and care homes has been observed  (Department  
of Health, 1994; Musher and others  , 2007). IPCT  s should take a measured approach when  
assessing potential outbreaks of CDI  . Apparent increases in cases may be influenced by factors  
such as improved case ascertainment, heightened clinical awareness, or changes in patient  
population (for example  more high-  risk admissions). These may result in clusters or pseudo-  
outbreaks that do not reflect true transmission events. Outbreak declaration should be based on  
local surveillance data, epidemiological investigation, and in accordance with current guidelines.  
[2025 expert review: retained with updated text.]

## section 3: strategies to prevent cdi
1. Existing guidelines and recommendations a. Published guidelines for the management of CDI are few, and only some address CDI prevention. 22,25-27
i. Most data published on CDI prevention are from before-after studies conducted in response to outbreaks. Often, several concomitant interventions are performed, making it difficult to determine the relative importance of one intervention compared with another. Before-after studies are also limited by time-related biases that are difficult to adjust for in the absence of a control group or properly conducted analyses, such as interrupted time series analysis. 30,31 However, 2 recent studies have used these techniques, demonstrating the importance of an-timicrobial stewardship and its role in preventing CDI. 31,32 b. Less is known about the mechanisms and prevention of C. difficile transmission, compared with other antimi-crobial-resistant gram-positive organisms, such as MRSA and vancomycin-resistant enterococcus (VRE). Although these 3 organisms have many common epidemiologic char-acteristics, C. difficile and VRE, in particular, share risk factors for transmission. 33 The major difference among these 3 organisms is that C. difficile forms spores, whereas the other 2 do not. The formation of spores has novel (as yet unknown) implications for methods of hand hygiene and environmental disinfection, because C. difficile spores are resistant to the bactericidal effects of alcohol and most hospital disinfectants. i. Methods of reducing the risk of CDI if the organism is encountered by the patient (a) Follow antimicrobial usage restriction and stewardship guidelines.
ii. Methods of preventing the patient from being ex-posed to C. difficile (disinfection and barrier methods) (a) Avoid the use of electronic thermometers; the handles become contaminated with C. difficile.

(b) Use dedicated patient care items and equip-ment; if items must be shared, clean and disinfect the equipment between patients. (c) Use full barrier precautions (gowns and gloves) for contact with patients with CDI and for contact with their body substances and environment (contact precautions). (d) Place patients with CDI in private rooms, if available; give isolation preference to patients with fecal incontinence if room availability is limited. (e) Perform meticulous hand hygiene based on Centers for Disease Control and Prevention or World Health Organization guidelines before and after en-tering the room of a patient with CDI, with soap and water or an alcohol-based hand-hygiene product (in routine settings or settings of endemicity). Perform hand hygiene with soap and water preferentially, in-stead of alcohol hand hygiene products, after caring for a patient with CDI in outbreak settings or settings of hyperendemicity. Ensure that proper hand-hygiene techniques are used when hand washing with soap and water is employed. 34 (f) Perform environmental decontamination of rooms housing patients with CDI, using sodium hypochlorite (household bleach) diluted 1 : 10 with water, in an outbreak setting or setting of hyper-endemicity. (g) Educate healthcare personnel and hospital ad-ministration about the clinical features, transmission, and epidemiology of CDI. d. Other important principles to be aware of when car-ing for patients with CDI include the following: 22,25-27
i. Perform testing for C. difficile only on unformed diarrheal stools (toxin testing of formed stool is strongly discouraged).
ii. Do not give prophylactic antimicrobial CDI ther-apy (eg, with metronidazole or vancomycin) to patients at high risk for CDI.
iii. Do not treat or attempt to decolonize asymptom-atic C. difficile carriers. Antimicrobial therapy is not ef-fective for decolonization.
iv. Do not conduct repeated testing for C. difficile if a patient has had a stool sample positive for C. difficile,
unless symptoms resolved with treatment and then re-turned after treatment (ie, do not perform test of cure in patients successfully treated for CDI). 2. Infrastructure requirements a. Trained infection prevention and control personnel

i. Infection prevention and control personnel must be able to identify patients with CDI as soon as possible after their condition is diagnosed. This is necessary to ensure that patients are placed under contact precautions in a timely fashion. These data can also be used to cal-culate CDI rates. c. Ability to place patients with CDI under contact precautions
i. Contact precautions require the ability to place pa-tients in a private room (preferably) or to cohort patients with CDI, as well as to place materials necessary for compliance with contact precautions (eg, gowns and gloves) in an easily accessible space outside of the pa-tient’s room.
ii. Place a sign indicating that the patient is under contact precautions outside of the patient’s room.
iii. If there is a limited number of single-bed rooms, patients with stool incontinence should preferentially be placed in these rooms.

**Dr. Damon Tweedy:**Okay, hold on. Stop again, s top again,c ome on. S o you mean like a Confederate monument with B lack folks in it? That sounds kind of crazy to me.
**Dr. Jeff Baker****:**This is why I'm in history. You can't make this stuff up. B ut it sounded crazy to M oore as well, okay.So M oore and his allies and in the NC Mutual suggested to Duke that maybe a better way to honor those men would be to build a hospital for their descendants. And Duke was persuaded. He wrote a check. Black businesses wrote checks as well. And that's actually how Durham got itself Lincoln Ho spital. It opened its doors in 1901 with 50 beds and a policy of admitting patients without any regard to their ability to pay. This hospital became a tremendous source of pride to the local community.The staff, all Black, were focused on improving the health of Durham's African-American population. They created programs, public health programs, targeting maternal health and infectious diseases. They established health education programs, offered free emergency care to anyone
whether or not they could pay. That's going to be important to our story. And in addition, Lincoln c reated opportunities for Black doctors and nurses through the nursing residency and surgery programs at a time when there really we ren't that many opportunities for Black people in the south in healthcare.
**Dr. Damon Tweedy:**So I think one important lesson, just the story you're telling about Lincoln, Jeff, is that even to this day, if we are honest, there are a lot of stereotypes that persist when we talk about Black people, whether it's this sense of Black people not being e ducated or being lazy and lacking ingenuity and these sorts of things. And Lincoln's story really tells something totally the opposite, right?It's completely different from that. It showed how people could really create something from nothing,in the fac e of the most really terrible obstacles. And so it is a story of how can someone,create something from nothing--the agency, perseverance, whatever adjective you want to d escribe--I think it's a really important story for us to know.

**Dr. Jeff Baker:**This is a story, a powerful story of Black agency, and it's also a story of racial cooperation. In 1924, when Lincoln Hospital burned down, it was the newly created Duke Endowment that stepped in and provided basically half the funding to rebuild the hospi tal. The other half was provided by the Black community, and the Duke family would always see itself as having a connection to Lincoln Hospital. That's going to be important for our story too.
**Dr. Damon Tweedy:**And it was this hospital that Maltheus Avery was brought to in 1950 after his car accident.
**Dr. Jeff Baker:**That's right. So I think now we're ready to hear the story of Maltheus Avery. I think we have the stage set.

# DASON Digest
## Episodes
1.   18h ago ### Comment-based Stewardship Regarding Amp C Beta-lactamase Producing Organisms Episode Notes In this episode of the DASON Digest podcast, DASON Clinical Pharmacist Liaison Dr. April Dyer talks with us about a new publication in ASHE entitled "Reducing carbapenem use for low-risk AmpC-producing Enterobacterales: impact of a microbiology comment-based stewardship initiative." The open access article can be reviewed here: https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/antimicrobial-stewardship-and-healthcare-epidemiology/article/reducing-carbapenem-use-for-lowrisk-ampcproducing-enterobacterales-impact-of-a-microbiology-commentbased-stewardship-initiative/6B896A60FC0144A27A78F1E7A2700EB7 For more information about DASON, please visit: https://dason.medicine.duke.edu/ 13m   
2.   Oct 9 ### Emerging Data in Antimicrobial Spectrum Scoring Episode Notes Join ID fellow Arielle Cohen as she speaks with Dr. Dan Ilges, Associate Professor of Pharmacy and Clinical Specialist Pharmacist at Mayo Clinic in Arizona, and Dr. Ryan Stevens, Associate Professor of Pharmacy and Medicine at Mayo Clinic in Rochester, Minnesota, about their recent editorial commentary, Settling the Score: The Past Present, and Future of Antimicrobial Scoring, written in response to the recent publication by Mackow et al: Development and Application of an Anaerobic Activity Index, published in CID. They focus on opportunities and challenges within antimicrobial spectrum scoring, including research, clinical, and stewardship program applications. For more information about DASON, please visit: https://dason.medicine.duke.edu/ 39m

scrubbed. Gentle scrubbing may be useful in wounds older than 3–4 hours, even if they are clean, as it removes a glycoprotein matrix that may cover the wound and allows bacterial colonization. Debridement of devitalized tissue is paramount to reducing risk of infection. Scalpel excision of wound margins can be used in grossly contaminated wounds. Debridement is more relevant for infected wounds and hence more information is provided on debridement later in this chapter.

Management of Infected Wounds2 Infection is said to have occurred when bacterial numbers in wound overwhelm the immune response and clinical signs of infection appear. Risk of infection can be reduced by proper hand washing, infection control, wound cleansing and debridement. Protection of wounds from exogenous sources of contamination is important. Prevention of infection can enhance wound healing and reduce hospital stay and cost. In presence of systemic and clinical signs of infection, systemic antimicrobial therapy should be considered. Culture swab is required only if clinical signs of spreading infection are present such as pyrexia, heat, redness, swelling or pain. One must review antibiotic choice and duration when swab results are available. Changing of dressing daily or alternate days, depending on exudate is important. If purulent material or foul odor is present, more frequent cleansing and possibly debridement are required. Topical antimicrobials: Topical antiseptic agents are commonly used, but suffer from certain disadvantages. They have been shown to retard wound healing.15,16 Topical anti­biotics, particularly neomycin and gentamicin are frequent causes of contact dermatitis. However, certain topical antimicrobial agents are useful and are mentioned below: zz Silver dressings, e.g. silver sulfadiazine: Silver compounds are widely used in burn care, being effective against Staphylococcus aureus and Pseudomonas aeruginosa, in a concentration as low as 10 mmol/L and possibly having an effect by enhancing epithelialisation.17 zz Povidone-iodine in low concentration as described above. zz Honey18 stimulates tissue growth and epithelialization, as well as reducing inflammation and infection, debriding and deodorizing wounds. 19 It is also effective against antibiotic resistant bacteria, including methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus.20 zz Cane sugar containing sucrose, which is not metabolized outside the gastrointestinal tract, prevents bacterial growth by decreasing available water, and it has also been claimed to stimulate granulation tissue.21 zz Metronidazole which acts against anaerobes.

Wound closure has definite role in management of clean wounds-clean wounds should be closed immediately to allow healing by primary intention. A closed dressing exposes the wound continuously to proteinases, chemotactic, complement and growth factors in the surrounding fluid, which may be otherwise lost in case the wound is left exposed. The electrical gradient required for stimulation of fibroblasts and epithelial cell migration is maintained and further trauma to the wound is avoided by this physical barrier. However, contami­nated and infected wounds should not be closed but left open to heal by secondary intention. In treating clean contaminated wounds and clean wounds that are more than 6–8 hours old, one must manage with surgical toilet, the wound left open and then closed 48 hours later. Negative Pressure Wound Therapy Negative pressure wound therapy (NPWT) or vacuumassisted closure (VAC) has played a major role as a bridge to reconstruction. It is a significant, clinically proven advancement in wound care that promotes active wound healing at the cellular level through negative pressure. Pressure used is negative pressure or sub-atmospheric pressure (100–125 mm Hg) in a continuous or intermittent manner. The intermittent negative pressure is delivered at wound site through a porous dressing, which applies mechanical forces known as macro strain (physical response) and micro strain (biological response) and subsequently removes exudates by an electromechanical pump.

PRIMARY WOUND REPAIR3 Primary closure requires that clean tissue is approximated without tension. Primary closure is done by suturing, wound adhesives or staples. Injudicious closure of a contaminated wound will promote infection and delay healing. These have been dealt with in detail in the chapter on sutures. Body hair entangled in sutures and staples or buried inside the wound can alter the healing process and increase the risk of infection. It is important to understand that routine hair removal by shaving before suturing can lead to poor outcomes. If hair has to be removed, scissors or clippers should be used. It has also been shown that use
of clean non-sterile gloves are not inferior to sterile gloves in terms of infection control. The hair apposition technique (HAT) for scalp wounds and lacerations should be considered for the repair of scalp lacerations that are non-crush injuries less than 10 cm long with regular wound edges, minimal contamination, without evidence of underlying skull fractures and with an intact galea in patients with hair strands longer than 3 cm. These techniques are associated with less scarring, fewer overall complications, shorter procedural time, lower pain scores, and substantially lower costs than standard suturing and stapler techniques. The HAT technique consists of twisting together three to seven strands of hair on either side of the wound. The two bundles of hair are then interlocked in a 360° revolution and a small drop of tissue adhesive can be applied. The hair is not tied. This same process is repeated as needed for the entire length of the wound. The glue will break down and the hair will unravel by itself after 7–10 days.24

TISSUE ADHESIVES (2-OCTYL CYANOACRYLATE)25 The commonly used wound adhesives include 2-butyl cyanoacrylate and 2-octyl cyanoacrylate. 2-Octyl cyanoacrylate use is often correlated with laceration repair, which is certainly a popular application. However, it is also widely used for operative incision repair. Sutureless pediatric circumcisions, cleft lip repair and upper eyelid blepharoplasties are a few innovative surgical incision closures that have been facilitated with the use of 2-octyl cyanoacrylate. It is most commonly used in dermatology to hold in place punch and suction blister grafts. Cosmetic results with 2-octyl cyanoacrylate equals those of sutures. Tips on use of 2-octyl cyanoacrylate are in Box 3. More details can be found in the chapter on wound and closure materials.

Methods to Mitigate Risk of LAST The American Society of Regional Anesthesia and Pain Medicine recommends following techniques to reduce the risk of LAST: 107 1. Minimalistic approach: Use of just adequate dose of LAA is better. Lean body mass is a better index for dose calculation than whole body weight in overweight/ obese individuals. Whenever combination of LAAs is used, lesser doses of each should be used as the side effects can accrue. 2. Choosing right LAA: LAA with higher CC/CNS ratios should be preferred. 3. Safe technique of administration: Aspirate before injecting so as to confirm that needle is not intravascular. Administer LAA as small boluses slowly rather than depositing large doses in a single shot. Maintaining a gap of one circulation time viz., 30–45 seconds between these boluses is a safe practice. 4. Use of marker of intravascular injection: A test dose of epinephrine 5µg/ml of LAA has been used to know the expected response, adverse reaction in case of intravascular injection. An intravascular injection of 3ml of LAA with epinephrine (1:200000) viz., 15 µg of epinephrine causes tachycardia (10 beats/min) and rise in systolic pressure by 15 mm Hg. But this may not be appreciated in elderly patients and those on beta blockers, sedated or under general anesthesia. 5. Ultrasound guided administration of peripheral nerve blocks: this avoids intravascular injection of LAA.
Management of LAST Most important aspect of management is early recognition of LAST! Monitor the vitals for 30 mins after administration of LAA and keep speaking to patient to recognize any early CNS side effects. Any alteration of mental function or variations of cardiac parameters is LAST. Like in any hypersensitivity or toxicity reactions, maintenance of airway, breathing and circulation is critical for resuscitation of an individual with LAST. Seizures can be effectively treated with benzodiazepines and if refractory may require succinylcholine (see Table 4). However, these need anesthetist or an intensivists intervention. CNS or cardiac complications necessitate advanced life support and appropriate timely intervention. Epinephrine ropivacaine, procaine, tetracaine).109

Drug Fever Drug fever was noted with EMLA but not plain 2% lidocaine jelly. Drug fever correlated with increase in serum IL-6 levels.110
Pseudobullous Dermatosis Both intraepidermal (subcorneal and suprabasal) as well as subepidermal clefting have been observed with EMLA application. Epidermal necrosis and multifocal clefting
Chapter 12: Local Anesthesia was more common with genital lesions secondary to EMLA application.111,112 Various adverse reactions noted with EMLA are erythema, edema, pain, allergic contact dermatitis, contact urticaria, purpura, post inflammatory hyperpigmentation and skin necrosis when applied to leg ulcers in patients with disordered microcirculation.113-116 Loss of vision has been documented during eyelid infiltration secondary to corneal perforation.117
Lipid Resuscitation Intravenous lipids have long been used for parenteral nutrition. It is an emulsion composed of egg phospholipids or soyabean oil in water. It has also been used to treat systemic toxicity of LAA (LAST) and referred as Intravenous lipid emulsion therapy and Lipid rescue. Commonly 20% emulsions are used for this purpose. Among various preparations available, Intralipid™ has maximum studies.
Mechanism of Action of Intravenous Lipids Various mechanisms have been hypothesized and include,118,119 1. Lipid sink: Lipid soluble LAA agents in circulation or tissue binding sites are attracted and absorbed by the intravenous lipids. 2. Influence on cardiac myocyte fatty acid metabolism: LAA inhibit fatty acid metabolism in heart and intravenous lipids counteract this by being an exogenous source of energy. 3. Acts as a positive inotrope 4. Relieves the sodium channel (Nav 1.5) by the drug 5. Regulate carnitine transport, thereby improving fatty acid metabolism in cardiac muscles.

Method of Use Initially a loading dose of 1.5 mL/kg is administered over 5 mins and subsequently a slow infusion of 0.25 mL/kg/min (i.e., about 18 mL/min if patient is 70 kg) is administered over 30–60 mins. If the hypotension persists, then one or two additional boluses are administered and the dose of continuous infusion is doubled (0.5 mL/kg/ min). Continuous infusion is continued for 10 mins after the CVS stability. Maximum recommended dose is 10 mL/ kg in initial 30 mins. Adverse effects of lipid resuscitation include alteration of laboratory tests (renal and liver function test, electrolytes, creatine kinase and total proteins; this tends to persists for 24 hours after administration of intravenous lipids), pancreatitis, pulmonary dysfunction, acute renal failure and deep vein thrombosis.120
Positioning of Lipid Resuscitiation for LAST Even though intravenous lipids have found to reverse CVS and CNS adverse effects of LAAs in some reports, lipid
resuscitation cannot be used as first line therapy for LAST. It can be used when all other resuscitative efforts fail. It can be used for treating toxicity due to lipophilic drugs viz., bupivacaine and can be considered for treating toxicity due to other LAAs, amitriptyline and bupropion.121.122

CHEST PAIN Chest pain may be a manifestation of not only coronary arterial ischemia but also anxiety. However, fear, stress of pain and procedure can also precipitate an acute myocardial infarction in any patient prone for ischemia. Although most dermatologic surgical procedures are day care and performed in young healthy individuals, at times, if a high-risk patient is being subjected to esthetic surgery, thorough evaluation would be mandatory. If a patient complains of chest pain during the procedure, place the patient supine and check the vitals. Activate physician/emergency medical services. Record an electrocardiogram, which may be compared against the basal. If you are suspecting coronary ischemia, a tablet of nitroglycerine 5 mg should be placed immediately under the tongue. One must be aware of possible headache and hypotension following this measure. An intravenous (IV) cannula should be inserted immediately (if not already done) and a patent IV line is important for further management. If with these measures the chest pain settles and the patient is hemodynamically stable, one can proceed with the surgery. If the pain is unabated and electro­cardiographic changes persist or worsen, the scheduled procedure should be deferred with. Patient may undergo the scheduled procedure after a consult with a cardiologist. Patients at risk for myocardial ischemia should be thoroughly evaluated and medically optimized prior to the procedure. In the author’s opinion, it may be wise to have ‘monitored anesthesia care’ for all patients.
BLEEDING A major surgical bleeder is rare in cutaneous surgeries. A patient receiving antiplatelet medications for concomitant comorbidities may pose special issues. Such patients may be better prepared by stopping the antiplatelet medication
Chapter 18: Management of Dermatosurgical Emergencies at least for 2 weeks prior to the planned procedure. Although the hemorrhage associated with cutaneous surgery may not be life threatening, its other effects such as causing a menacing hematoma and lifting of flaps compromising their viability may be of nuisance value.17,18 For more information on hemostasis reader is referred to the chapter on Hemostasis.

ACUTE STROKE Patients on antiplatelet or antithrombotic therapy19 and their sudden discontinuation, patients with carotid bruit, patients with prior history of stroke, patients with cardiovascular disease are all at potential risk for stroke.18 Pre-procedural evaluation by a physician or a neurologist has to be considered in such patients. During the procedure, the dermatologist’s role chiefly concerns the detection phase of a sudden neurologic deficit. This may include an alteration in consciousness (confusion, coma and seizures), aphasia, dysarthria, facial weakness or asymmetry, extremity weakness, paralysis, sensory loss, ataxia, visual loss or vertigo. Immediately activate the physician or emergency medical services. A definitive hospital-based intervention must occur within 3 hours of the onset of the stroke symptoms to be beneficial. Meanwhile attend to the ABCs (airway, breathing, circulation) of resuscitation and monitor vitals and manage accordingly till the physician arrives.
STATUS EPILEPTICUS Dermatologists do encounter disease with potential epileptic manifestations in conditions such as tuberous sclerosis, systemic lupus erythematosus (Box 5). It is wise to obtain any past history of seizures and antiseizure medications.20 If the patients are epileptic on treatment, one should advise them to continue the treatment until the day of surgery. Box 5: Management of status epilepticus. • Stop the ongoing procedure. First priority is always the maintenance of airway. Use an oral or naso­pharyn­geal airway as and when required (inserting these airways are out of the routine for dermatological surgeons, it is advisable for them to learn the insertion of these airways from their anesthesia or critical care colleagues) • If available, oxygen can be delivered by face mask • Monitor the vital signs • Place the patient on a soft, flat surface away from sharp objects • Look for and prevent tongue bite • If seizures has stopped and the patient is breathing and has a pulse, place the patient in a recovery position (modified lateral position).It will allow the clearance of any pooled secretions • Secure a peripheral intravenous line and send blood sample for blood glucose, serum electrolytes • The benzodiazepine midazolam or lorazepam 1–2 mg or diazepam 5–10 mg intravenously will stop the seizures • Call for physician and evaluate for seizures etiology and further management options

COLLAPSE Most commonly syncope, anaphylaxis, hypoglycemia and cardiac arrest are reasons for collapse of a patient. These issues may be addressed as discussed in the chapter. However, associated with a vasomotor collapse are some of the key issues mentioned below which need attention.
HYPOTENSION Low blood pressure may result from bleeding, syncope, anaphylaxis, acute myocardial infarction, and secondary to medications such as sedatives/anesthetic agents. Patient may complain of giddiness (or orthostatic hypotension).
Management Place the patient in supine position and check vital signs such as, pulse rate and blood pressure. Treat the underlying cause. Tachycardia with low blood pressure indicates blood loss, start the patient on intravenous fluid crystalloids. Ringer’s lactate 5–10 mL/kg bolus over 15 minutes can be administered and the blood pressure checked. If good response continues, intravenous fluid (Ringer’s lactate) at the rate of 2–4 mL/kg/hour may be continued. If there is no response to the fluids, check for continued blood loss; send a sample of blood for checking the hemoglobin level. In the absence of matched donor blood, it is vital to maintain the circulating blood volume by administration of colloids such as starch solutions. More damage might be caused by allowing hypovolemia than anemia.21,22 If hypotension persists, one should seek a physician’s opinion and have a provision for starting an inotropic infusion such as injection dopamine 5 µg/kg/ min should be commenced.
HYPERTENSION Known hypertensives, elderly, female, anxious patients are prone for increased blood pressure during the procedure. Accelerated hypertensive patients can also present with giddiness, severe headache. Optimization of blood pressure for known hypertensives, reassuring the patients, premedicant such as alprazolam, sedatives such as midazolam, lorazepam would help in the control of blood pressure. Involvement of a physician would be helpful if basic interventions do not reduce the blood pressure.

Dermatological Procedures and Infection Control Infections after dermatological procedures are not only rare but usually insignificant. These procedures are majorly aesthetic ones and these ‘patients’ do not suffer from any major systemic illnesses; the expectation about outcomes are usually high. Absence of infection after the procedure is one such expectation. The dermatologic surgeon must attend to the infection control measures in providing clean

Section 1: Basic Principles of Cutaneous Surgery ambience while conducting the procedure, using standard precautions, preoperative decolonization of methicillinresistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) and surgical prophylaxis. Postprocedure, the patients may be advised about care of the wound and reporting early if signs of infection come up. Preoperative preparation: It is a common knowledge that Staphylococcus aureus is a common cutaneous com­ mensal; it is impossible to eradicate it. While conducting surgical operations requiring skin incision, the colony count of these organisms have to be reduced. The methods to achieve this are: a. Preoperative chlorhexidine 2% v/v wash: The patients have to bathe twice daily for 3 preoperative days. This solution cannot be applied over the scalp and face. Those wishing to operate on the scalp and the face may use triclosan solution. b. Intranasal mupirocin ointment: All the surgical patients must be requested to use mupirocin ointment twice daily for 5 days preoperatively. This decolonizes the nasal mucosa of MRSA. c. Surgical preparation: It is recommended that we must use chlorhexidine tincture 2% w/v to prepare the skin. This solution has been found to be superior to using povidone iodine; its residual action is longer than that of povidone iodine. Whether chlorhexidine or povidone iodine is used, one must wait for at least 3 minutes prior to incision. The commonly found practice of ‘rubbing off’ excess solution using a gauze should be shunned and instead, the solution must be allowed to dry by itself; only then the antibacterial effect is maximized. d. Preoperative surgical prophylaxis: It is recommended by Center for Disease Control and Prevention that a single dose of first or second generation cephalosporin be administered intravenously 15–60 minutes prior to incision. Administering 1.5 g of cefuroxime suffices in most adults. If the surgery continues beyond 4 hours, a similar dose must be administered. e. Normoglycemia and normothermia: It has been shown that intraoperative blood sugar and temperature maintenance is absolutely essential. Cutaneous surgeries are no exception to these recommendations.

Chapter 23: Simple Excisions suture removal, excellent cosmetic results can be obtained. A well-approximated, everted wound with minimal suture tracking is ideal outcome of simple excision surgery. Various modifications of suture techniques can be used in cutaneous surgery with each technique having its advantages and disadvantages to achieve best possible cosmetic results.13
OTHER SIMPLE EXCISION METHODS The standard elliptical excision may not be suitable for excision of skin lesions in certain age groups and anatomical sites. In such situation, different excision techniques are utilized to give good cosmetic result with minimal scarring.
Circular Excision and Purse-String Closure It is an effective technique used for excision of circular facial skin lesions in children. Apart from infantile hemangioma (at any stage of evolution), other skin lesions treated successfully with this technique include Spitz nevus, pyogenic granuloma, pilomatricoma, vascular malformations and pigmented nevus. 14 In infantile hemangioma, circular excision and purse-string closure converts large circular lesion into a small ellipsoid scar by significantly reducing the transverse and longitudinal dimensions of the lesion. If required, the ellipsoid scar can be revised subsequently to a linear scar of same length. Hence, the smallest possible scar with minimal distortion of surrounding tissue can be achieved by this method.15 However, to avoid pleat formation, this method is not indicated for lesions on the free margins such as periorbital region, or on the upper or lower lip.16

Intralesional Excision and Primary Closure The long scar and dog ear formation of elliptical excision and pleat formation of circular excision can be overcome by intralesional excision and primary closure. Infantile hemangiomas, involuting or involuted, are suitable for intralesional excision because of expanded dome-shaped tissue, and excess and redundant skin which permit easy scooping of fibrofatty tissue and closure of wound edge without tension, respectively. In this method, intralesional elliptical resection with dull apical angles and primary closure is performed without extending the incision into the normal skin. A small outermost portion of the lesion is preserved intentionally. If the residual lesion is large, then the same procedure can be repeated 2–3 times at the interval of 3 months each. Intralesional excision is not indicated for hemangiomas in proliferative phase because of excessive intraoperative bleeding and brittle residual tissue.16
POSTOPERATIVE CARE AND WOUND DRESSING Postoperatively the wound is cleaned to remove blood and residual antiseptic. Dressing is applied in four layers comprising of occlusive ointment, a nonadherent gauze material, an absorbent cushion made of cotton covered with gauze material on both sides and adhesive tape to secure the dressing (Fig. 20). Dressing must kept dry all the time and the patient is instructed accordingly. If the dressing gets soiled it has to be replaced immediately. First redressing is to be done after 24 hours. The patient is trained to do subsequent dressings on his own till suture removal.
COMPLICATIONS AND THEIR MANAGEMENT3 With good planning technique and aseptic precautions, complications in cutaneous surgery are very rare. Patients should be warned and informed about them preoperatively. The surgeon should be able to recognize and manage them whenever they occur.
Hematoma Hematomas are seen within 24–48 hours after surgery and they manifest as swelling, erythema and tenderness at wound site. Hematomas are evacuated promptly by partially or completely opening the wound. Resuturing can be done if hematoma develops within early 24 hours provided the wound is not infected. Otherwise the wound is kept open and allowed to heal by second intention. Scar revision can be done at later date. Very small hematomas need not be opened; they can be managed with warm compresses till resolution.

Methods of Dog-ear Correction Before planning the removal of dog-ear, it is often beneficial to partially close the wound edges to determine whether a tissue protrusion will form.
Dehiscence The wound pulls apart in dehiscence usually as a result of underlying infection and/or hematoma. These causes should be promptly managed allowing the wound to heal by second intention. Delayed scar revision can be done at a later date.
Linear Repair This is simple, easy to perform and useful when it is desirable to extend the excision in a straight line. The apex of tissue protrusion is elevated with a skin-hook to define the geometry of tissue protrusion in the shape of a standing cone. The apex of the cone is drawn to one side so that the base of the tissue protrusion is in line with the long axis of the anticipated wound closure. The base is incised and undermined to free up a triangular wedge of tissue. The triangular section is then draped over the underlying wound edge with gentle tension and the base is incised over the line of closure. The wound is then repaired in a straight line. Other methods of dog-ear repair are curved repair, hockey stick repair, l-shaped repair, T-shaped repair and N-plasty repair.3
Necrosis Necrosis is a rare complication of simple excision surgery. It occurs only if the wound is closed under high tension thereby compromising the vascularity of the wound margins. The course of action should be suture removal, debridement of the necrotic tissue and allowing the wound to heal by second intention. Corrective scar revision is undertaken at a later date.

Dog-ear A skin protrusion present at the end of excision is commonly referred to as a dog-ear. These protrusions are caused by the presence of redundant skin at the ends or dressing sites of an excision. The amount of tissue protrusion formed in a given wound is fundamentally determined by the amount of rotation, advancement and intrinsic tissue elasticity of the surrounding skin. The local surface contours also contribute to the final degree of tissue protrusion. Circumferential closures performed on highly convex surfaces, such as the arm, will result in tissue protrusions at the end of the closure. If excess subcutaneous fat is present at the apex of an excision, the resultant elevation of the angle of closure may mimic a tissue protrusion. Removal of excess

Management of Infected Wounds2 Infection is said to have occurred when bacterial numbers in wound overwhelm the immune response and clinical signs of infection appear. Risk of infection can be reduced by proper hand washing, infection control, wound cleansing and debridement. Protection of wounds from exogenous sources of contamination is important. Prevention of infection can enhance wound healing and reduce hospital stay and cost. In presence of systemic and clinical signs of infection, systemic antimicrobial therapy should be considered. Culture swab is required only if clinical signs of spreading infection are present such as pyrexia, heat, redness, swelling or pain. One must review antibiotic choice and duration when swab results are available. Changing of dressing daily or alternate days, depending on exudate is important. If purulent material or foul odor is present, more frequent cleansing and possibly debridement are required. Topical antimicrobials: Topical antiseptic agents are commonly used, but suffer from certain disadvantages. They have been shown to retard wound healing.15,16 Topical anti­biotics, particularly neomycin and gentamicin are frequent causes of contact dermatitis. However, certain topical antimicrobial agents are useful and are mentioned below: zz Silver dressings, e.g. silver sulfadiazine: Silver compounds are widely used in burn care, being effective against Staphylococcus aureus and Pseudomonas aeruginosa, in a concentration as low as 10 mmol/L and possibly having an effect by enhancing epithelialisation.17 zz Povidone-iodine in low concentration as described above. zz Honey18 stimulates tissue growth and epithelialization, as well as reducing inflammation and infection, debriding and deodorizing wounds. 19 It is also effective against antibiotic resistant bacteria, including methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus.20 zz Cane sugar containing sucrose, which is not metabolized outside the gastrointestinal tract, prevents bacterial growth by decreasing available water, and it has also been claimed to stimulate granulation tissue.21 zz Metronidazole which acts against anaerobes.

Wound closure has definite role in management of clean wounds-clean wounds should be closed immediately to allow healing by primary intention. The hair apposition technique (HAT) for scalp wounds and lacerations should be considered for the repair of scalp lacerations that are non-crush injuries less than 10 cm long with regular wound edges, minimal contamination, without evidence of underlying skull fractures and with an intact galea in patients with hair strands longer than 3 cm. These techniques are associated with less scarring, fewer overall complications, shorter procedural time, lower pain scores, and substantially lower costs than standard suturing and stapler techniques. The HAT technique consists of twisting together three to seven strands of hair on either side of the wound. The two bundles of hair are then interlocked in a 360° revolution and a small drop of tissue adhesive can be applied. The hair is not tied. This same process is repeated as needed for the entire length of the wound. The glue will break down and the hair will unravel by itself after 7–10 days.24

Methods to Mitigate Risk of LAST The American Society of Regional Anesthesia and Pain Medicine recommends following techniques to reduce the risk of LAST: 107 1. Minimalistic approach: Use of just adequate dose of LAA is better. Lean body mass is a better index for dose calculation than whole body weight in overweight/ obese individuals. Whenever combination of LAAs is used, lesser doses of each should be used as the side effects can accrue. 2. Choosing right LAA: LAA with higher CC/CNS ratios should be preferred. 3. Safe technique of administration: Aspirate before injecting so as to confirm that needle is not intravascular. Administer LAA as small boluses slowly rather than depositing large doses in a single shot. Maintaining a gap of one circulation time viz., 30–45 seconds between these boluses is a safe practice. 4. Use of marker of intravascular injection: A test dose of epinephrine 5µg/ml of LAA has been used to know the expected response, adverse reaction in case of intravascular injection. An intravascular injection of 3ml of LAA with epinephrine (1:200000) viz., 15 µg of epinephrine causes tachycardia (10 beats/min) and rise in systolic pressure by 15 mm Hg. But this may not be appreciated in elderly patients and those on beta blockers, sedated or under general anesthesia. 5. Ultrasound guided administration of peripheral nerve blocks: this avoids intravascular injection of LAA.
Management of LAST Most important aspect of management is early recognition of LAST! Monitor the vitals for 30 mins after administration of LAA and keep speaking to patient to recognize any early CNS side effects. Any alteration of mental function or variations of cardiac parameters is LAST. Like in any hypersensitivity or toxicity reactions, maintenance of airway, breathing and circulation is critical for resuscitation of an individual with LAST. Seizures can be effectively treated with benzodiazepines and if refractory may require succinylcholine (see Table 4). However, these need anesthetist or an intensivists intervention. CHEST PAIN Chest pain may be a manifestation of not only coronary arterial ischemia but also anxiety. However, fear, stress of pain and procedure can also precipitate an acute myocardial infarction in any patient prone for ischemia. Although most dermatologic surgical procedures are day care and performed in young healthy individuals, at times, if a high-risk patient is being subjected to esthetic surgery, thorough evaluation would be mandatory. If a patient complains of chest pain during the procedure, place the patient supine and check the vitals. Activate physician/emergency medical services. Record an electrocardiogram, which may be compared against the basal. If you are suspecting coronary ischemia, a tablet of nitroglycerine 5 mg should be placed immediately under the tongue. One must be aware of possible headache and hypotension following this measure. An intravenous (IV) cannula should be inserted immediately (if not already done) and a patent IV line is important for further management. If with these measures the chest pain settles and the patient is hemodynamically stable, one can proceed with the surgery. If the pain is unabated and electro­cardiographic changes persist or worsen, the scheduled procedure should be deferred with. Patient may undergo the scheduled procedure after a consult with a cardiologist. Patients at risk for myocardial ischemia should be thoroughly evaluated and medically optimized prior to the procedure. In the author’s opinion, it may be wise to have ‘monitored anesthesia care’ for all patients.
BLEEDING A major surgical bleeder is rare in cutaneous surgeries. A patient receiving antiplatelet medications for concomitant comorbidities may pose special issues. Such patients may be better prepared by stopping the antiplatelet medication

Although the hemorrhage associated with cutaneous surgery may not be life threatening, its other effects such as causing a menacing hematoma and lifting of flaps compromising their viability may be of nuisance value.17,18 For more information on hemostasis reader is referred to the chapter on Hemostasis.

ACUTE STROKE Patients on antiplatelet or antithrombotic therapy19 and their sudden discontinuation, patients with carotid bruit, patients with prior history of stroke, patients with cardiovascular disease are all at potential risk for stroke.18 Pre-procedural evaluation by a physician or a neurologist has to be considered in such patients. During the procedure, the dermatologist’s role chiefly concerns the detection phase of a sudden neurologic deficit. This may include an alteration in consciousness (confusion, coma and seizures), aphasia, dysarthria, facial weakness or asymmetry, extremity weakness, paralysis, sensory loss, ataxia, visual loss or vertigo. Immediately activate the physician or emergency medical services. A definitive hospital-based intervention must occur within 3 hours of the onset of the stroke symptoms to be beneficial. Meanwhile attend to the ABCs (airway, breathing, circulation) of resuscitation and monitor vitals and manage accordingly till the physician arrives.
STATUS EPILEPTICUS Dermatologists do encounter disease with potential epileptic manifestations in conditions such as tuberous sclerosis, systemic lupus erythematosus (Box 5). It is wise to obtain any past history of seizures and antiseizure medications.20 If the patients are epileptic on treatment, one should advise them to continue the treatment until the day of surgery. Box 5: Management of status epilepticus. • Stop the ongoing procedure. First priority is always the maintenance of airway. Use an oral or naso­pharyn­geal airway as and when required (inserting these airways are out of the routine for dermatological surgeons, it is advisable for them to learn the insertion of these airways from their anesthesia or critical care colleagues) • If available, oxygen can be delivered by face mask • Monitor the vital signs • Place the patient on a soft, flat surface away from sharp objects • Look for and prevent tongue bite • If seizures has stopped and the patient is breathing and has a pulse, place the patient in a recovery position (modified lateral position).It will allow the clearance of any pooled secretions • Secure a peripheral intravenous line and send blood sample for blood glucose, serum electrolytes • The benzodiazepine midazolam or lorazepam 1–2 mg or diazepam 5–10 mg intravenously will stop the seizures • Call for physician and evaluate for seizures etiology and further management options

COLLAPSE Most commonly syncope, anaphylaxis, hypoglycemia and cardiac arrest are reasons for collapse of a patient. These issues may be addressed as discussed in the chapter. However, associated with a vasomotor collapse are some of the key issues mentioned below which need attention.
HYPOTENSION Low blood pressure may result from bleeding, syncope, anaphylaxis, acute myocardial infarction, and secondary to medications such as sedatives/anesthetic agents. Patient may complain of giddiness (or orthostatic hypotension).
Management Place the patient in supine position and check vital signs such as, pulse rate and blood pressure. Treat the underlying cause. Tachycardia with low blood pressure indicates blood loss, start the patient on intravenous fluid crystalloids. Ringer’s lactate 5–10 mL/kg bolus over 15 minutes can be administered and the blood pressure checked. If good response continues, intravenous fluid (Ringer’s lactate) at the rate of 2–4 mL/kg/hour may be continued. If there is no response to the fluids, check for continued blood loss; send a sample of blood for checking the hemoglobin level. In the absence of matched donor blood, it is vital to maintain the circulating blood volume by administration of colloids such as starch solutions. More damage might be caused by allowing hypovolemia than anemia.21,22 If hypotension persists, one should seek a physician’s opinion and have a provision for starting an inotropic infusion such as injection dopamine 5 µg/kg/ min should be commenced.
HYPERTENSION Known hypertensives, elderly, female, anxious patients are prone for increased blood pressure during the procedure. Accelerated hypertensive patients can also present with giddiness, severe headache. Optimization of blood pressure for known hypertensives, reassuring the patients, premedicant such as alprazolam, sedatives such as midazolam, lorazepam would help in the control of blood pressure. Involvement of a physician would be helpful if basic interventions do not reduce the blood pressure.

Dermatological Procedures and Infection Control Infections after dermatological procedures are not only rare but usually insignificant. These procedures are majorly aesthetic ones and these ‘patients’ do not suffer from any major systemic illnesses; the expectation about outcomes are usually high. Absence of infection after the procedure is one such expectation. The dermatologic surgeon must attend to the infection control measures in providing clean
